Hi Marissa,

Thanks again for the call yesterday. ForgingPath is finalizing the Dedicated purchase but before procurement signs off we need clarity on a couple of items tied to our latency-sensitive workloads. Two concrete asks:

1) Tail latency for reserved GPUs — your SLA references 99th/95th token latency windows for pooled requests. Our inference pattern is mix of short (<64 tokens) and long (>1024 tokens) requests; we need to understand how Redwood attributes tail latency when reserved nodes are serving a mix, and whether there is an adjustment or variance for sticky/multi-session KV cache workloads.

2) Queueing behavior during burst periods — if our reserved pool hits concurrency caps and requests are queued, what is the per-request timeout before Redwood falls back to either queued denial or routing to burst capacity (and how does that impact the SLA credit calculation)?

I attached a short doc with our traffic profile and highlighted the most concerning windows (FP_tail_cases). Happy to share more telemetry if helpful. Can your team propose a wording amendment or carveout so Procurement has something concrete to present to legal?

Alex — quick technical write-up below (keeping it high level, happy to jump on a short call).

1) Tail latency measurement for reserved pools- Our SLA computes token-level p95/p99 across requests served from your reserved pool only. For workloads that mix short and long sequences, two things matter:
  - batching and scheduling: we do continuous batching; short requests may be batched with long ones which can inflate token latency for the short request if it waits for the long token generation to progress.
  - KV cache stickiness: sessions that require a warm KV cache on specific nodes will preferentially target those nodes; if those nodes are saturated, tail latency can spike beyond nominal pooled SLOs.

Practical mitigation we recommend: a) pin long-sequence traffic to a dedicated subset of nodes (we can reserve a small 'long-tail' lane), or b) enable request-level priority headers so critical short requests are scheduled earlier in the batch window. Either approach reduces p99 exposure.

Proposed measurement variance: for customers who opt into a long-tail lane (reserved subset of your reserved capacity), we can provide a scoped SLO: p95/p99 calculated per-lane rather than across the whole pool. That becomes the basis for SLA crediting when the long-tail lane is active.

2) Queueing and burst fallback behavior- When a reserved pool hits concurrency limits we apply the following sequence:
  a) short grace backpressure window (configurable per-customer, default 200 ms) where we hold requests on the node to try to place them into the next batch;
  b) if still unscheduled, requests are queued at the pool level for up to "pool_timeout" (default 2.5s) before being routed to burst capacity (if purchased) or rejected with a 429.

SLA credit impact: only requests that were served (i.e., produced tokens) from your reserved pool count toward the reserved pool SLO. If a request is routed to burst capacity and served there, it is excluded from reserved-pool SLO computation; credit mechanisms instead look at overall availability of reserved capacity during the billing window.

Draft contract language (suggestion):
  "For workloads with heterogeneous sequence-length characteristics, Redwood agrees to provide per-lane SLO computation upon customer request. Requests routed to non-reserved burst capacity are excluded from reserved-pool SLO calculations. Queueing timeouts and grace durations are configurable; default values are 200 ms (node-level hold) and 2.5 s (pool-level queue)."

I can attach a short example with your traffic slices mapped to lanes — that will make procurement/legal comfortable. Want me to produce that and include a redline for your SOW?

Cheers,
Ben
